short: Augustus's imperial bodyguard became powerful enough to make and unmake emperors.
full:
Augustus formalised the Praetorian Guard around 27 BCE as an elite unit of roughly nine cohorts, drawn from Italian citizens and paid substantially more than ordinary legionaries, tasked with protecting the emperor and maintaining a Roman military presence near the capital, where legions were otherwise forbidden. Sejanus, prefect under Tiberius, consolidated the guard into a single barracks, the Castra Praetoria, and turned it into a genuine political force.

Over the following centuries the guard repeatedly decided imperial succession by acclamation, assassination or auction, most notoriously selling the throne to Didius Julianus in 193. Its support for the usurper Maxentius against Constantine proved fatal: after Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312, he disbanded the guard permanently, demolished its barracks, and dispersed its soldiers to frontier units, ending an institution that had outlasted and outmanoeuvred more than two dozen emperors.
